11/20. I consider myself an armchair historian, but the American Civil War has never interested me much. While a major event to Americans who never had a similar wide-sweeping war on their home soil, there were more important (and interesting) things going on in Europe, Africa and East Asia at that time.

The US was one of the four strongest countries in the world as early as 1850 after the acquisition of Mexican territory. By the 1860s probably only Britain was stronger. The war had enormous implications for world history as the US victory over the Confederacy enabled a future American hegemony.

That's the most obvious impact and it is very hard to cite something of greater world-historical importance in that period. One could argue it had enormous global social impact to a somewhat lesser extent - especially in the longer term. In the 19th century the US epitomized dynamism in any case.

I wouldn't say anything was going on in Asia that was on par for example. The things that come to mind there were the opening of Japan (itself prompted by the US), the Opium Wars, and I guess a weakening Ottoman state participating in the Crimean War. The scramble for Africa was still some years off as well.

The CW obviously had great national impact, and indirectly global impact by keeping the US united, but it wasn't exciting as far as wars go. The Union had twice as much population as the Confederates, most of the industry, and no serious risk of foreign interference, and it was a foregone conclusion that the South would get overwhelmed by sheer numbers within some years.

The race for Africa started a few years later, but still fell in the same mid-to-late 19th century time frame.

And yes, I was thinking about the forced opening of Japan and the sweeping changes this brought to Japanese society and its attitude about foreign countries. The Japanese Pacific expansionism of the 1920s and 1930s would probably not have happened.

The questions of foreign interference and a Southern victory were more up in the air. I'm not really the guy to ask on the Southern victory part as I have somewhat minimal interest in the relevant areas of study but I know enough about what I don't know to know that if a couple of things had gone the South's way at key moments it might have pulled off the improbable. On the foreign interference front the French and British were threats. How much is debatable but Napoleon III did go so far as to propose French-British intervention on the side of the South. Palmerston was interested but ended up refusing.

The war itself may have been less interesting than some of the bigger ones. But it was intense and high impact with bloody battles. It's been called the first industrial war and Sherman the first modern general. It's even been suggested that either side could have defeated any European army of the time in a land war.
